Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines

marriage noun

the married state

also married life, wedlock, matrimony, give in marriage, a happy marriage

classical

Caes. BG 1.3.4: fīliam suam in mātrimōnium dat
Plaut. Trin. 3.3.4: īre in mātrimōnium (Lewis & Short)

mātrimōnium, mātrimōniī n.

noun, second declension

marriage, wedlock

Marriage as a state, from māter. The man takes a wife in mātrimōnium dūcere (see marry), a father gives his daughter in mātrimōnium dare or collocāre, and in mātrimōnium petere is to ask for her hand (Lewis & Short). In the plural, after Augustus, it also means wives.

Other words

  • conjugium, conjugiī n. — marriage, the union of husband and wife

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.54: prīma societās in ipsō conjugiō est

    First any union or joining; of marriage, the bond of the couple themselves (Lewis & Short). In poetry and Tacitus also a husband or a wife (Verg. A. 3.296).

  • cōnūbium, cōnūbiī n. — marriage as a civil institution; the legal right to marry

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.54; Liv. 4.6.2 (Lewis & Short); Cic. Rep. 2.63; Liv. 4.1.1, of the right to intermarry (Lewis & Short)

    Marriage regarded as a civil institution (Lewis & Short); hence the right to intermarry, which a law of the decemvirs denied between patricians and the plebs until a law of the plebs repealed it (Cic. Rep. 2.63).

Examples

  • eīque fīliam suam in mātrimōnium dat

    and gives him his daughter in marriageCaes. BG 1.3.4

  • prīma societās in ipsō conjugiō est, proxima in līberīs, deinde ūna domus, commūnia omnia

    the first bond of society is marriage itself, the next is children, then one household with everything sharedCic. Off. 1.54

  • Perenne conjugium animus, nōn corpus facit.

    It is the mind, not the body, that makes a lasting marriage.Publ. P 54

See also marry, wedding, husband, couple, propose, single.
